issues.description: Field Farm.animals: The problem statement and UML require Farm.animals to be a List<Animal> and explicitly instruct to initialize it with a new ArrayList<>() in the no-argument constructor. The solution implementation declares animals as a Queue<Animal> backed by a LinkedList and exposes getter/setter using Queue<Animal>. The template has no concrete animals field (contains a TODO placeholder to implement Farm). This mismatch between the required attribute type (List/ArrayList) and the solution's attribute type (Queue/LinkedList) can confuse students about the expected collection type, the correct getter/setter signatures, and which collection-specific methods to use (e.g., add vs offer, indexing, iteration expectations).
issues.suggestedFix: Align the implementation with the problem statement: change the Farm.animals field to type java.util.List<Animal>, initialize it in the no-arg constructor with new java.util.ArrayList<>(), and update the getter and setter signatures to use List<Animal>. Update addAnimal/feedAllAnimals/singFarmSong to iterate over the List (using add() to add animals). Alternatively, if the exercise intends to accept any Collection, modify the problem statement to remove the explicit ArrayList instruction and state that any Collection implementation is acceptable and specify the exact getter/setter types expected (e.g., Collection<Animal>).

issues.description: Concept: the Farm's collection of animals. Problem statement and UML explicitly require a List<Animal> implemented with an ArrayList (the instructions say "List, implemented using an ArrayList" and the UML shows animals: List<Animal>). Template: the Farm.java template contains a TODO to implement the Farm (no concrete collection declaration, but the task text instructs an ArrayList). Solution: the solution declares the field as "private Queue<Animal> animals;" and initializes it with "new LinkedList<>()". Why this is confusing: students reading the problem/UML will implement a List/ArrayList and expect List semantics and API; the solution uses a different interface (Queue) and implementation (LinkedList) with different method names/semantics (offer/poll vs add/get, FIFO behavior). This naming/type mismatch for the same conceptual entity (the farm's animals container) increases cognitive load and can cause test or grading mismatches or surprise when comparing template, problem text, and solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Keep the conceptual identifier consistent across artifacts. Preferred fix: modify the solution so the Farm field is declared as List<Animal> animals and initialized with new ArrayList<>() (import java.util.List and java.util.ArrayList), and update any getters/setters to use List<Animal>. Alternate fix: if Queue/LinkedList semantics were intended, update the problem statement and UML to explicitly require a Queue and LinkedList and adjust the task text accordingly so all materials use the same collection type.
